newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr stalemated, imports show some life.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr stalemated, imports show some life.

text.p: The Australian dollar showed scant sign of life at the midsession after its offshore bounce with dealers reporting negligible interest from customers.
"There's supposed to be a big seller above US$0.7380 and a buyer below US$0.7340 and everyone else is happy to leave it that way," said one fence sitting trader.

The June balance of goods and services showed the largest surplus ever but won little attention since almost all of it was due to the sale of Reserve Bank gold reserves and stripping that out the surplus was only A$164 million. But imports were up a healthy 8.0 percent, suggesting some more life in the economy.

By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local currency was idling at US$0.7370/75 from an early U$0.7364/69 and US$0.7360/65 late here Monday. It dipped as low as US$0.7335 offshore but the move was exagerrated by an illiquid market and the losses were soon recouped when modest bids appeared.

Dealers doubted the recent US$0.7310/7440 range would be troubled while the threat of another official rate cut overshadowed the market. Most expect the RBA to cut official rates by 0.5 point to 5.0 percent after its monthly board meeting on August 5. This would be the fifth easing since last July and, in a seminal event, take rates below those in the U.S.

Traders reckoned such a move was largely priced into the dollar given it had fallen more than four cents since the last easing on May 23, but the market was wary in case the RBA chose to surprise once again.

A larger cut, for instance could see the dollar testing US$0.7280 in a hurry while no move at all on August 6 would inspire speculation the easing cycle had ended and trigger a sharp short covering rally, perhaps back to US$0.7550.
Today's data provided little insight into what to expect, although the pickup in imports could be seen an early sign of recovering domestic demand.
The overall surplus on goods and services widened to A$1.96 billion from A$787 million in May, but A$1.8 billion of that reflected the RBA's sale of gold reserves which were included in exports.

Goods exports were thus up a huge 23 percent and, on the surface, promised a big contribution to GDP growth from net exports. However, the gold would be taken from stocks so exactly offsetting their contribution in the exports measure.
Imports of both consumer and capital goods rose 14 percent in June, with the former largely boosted by car imports and the latter by civil aircraft purchases.

The lift in imports was still nothing like as emphatic enough to make the market question its central rate assumptions, a conclusion analysts also expected to make about building approvals and retail trade data out tomorrow and Thursday.

The dollar was mixed on the crosses where all sorts of currents were at work. The A$ was sharply higher on the pound, which suffered massive profit taking overnight, at 0.4515/20 stg from 0.4453/58 late Monday but lost ground on a rallying Kiwi to NZ$1.1391/12 from NZ$1.1422/42. It was up a shade at 86.37/47 yen from 86.20/30 and unchanged in trade weighted terms at 57.6.
